title.en: Aponibolinayen and the Sun: Marriage in the House of Ini-init
title.zh: 阿波妮波莉納衍與太陽：伊尼伊尼特家中的姻緣

region.en: Abra Province, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (Tinguian homeland, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋西北阿布拉省（丁桂安故地，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tinguian oral epic-cycle tale; collected 1903-1908, published 1915 (Fay-Cooper Cole)

source.work: Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian: A Study in Philippine Folk-Lore (Field Museum, 1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun', pp. 33-40

summary.en: The siksiklat vine carries Aponibolinayen to the sky, where she hides in the betel-nut trees of Ini-init, the Sun, who goes up each morning to make the sun. With her magic she cooks a fish-stick into fish; he spies on the beautiful woman whose presence makes the house seem ablaze, chews betel with her — the quids of both turning to holeless agate beads, a sign they are kin — and they marry. When she insists on riding up with him, the heat melts her to oil; he bottles her and drops her by the well at Kaodanan, and she arrives home at last.
summary.zh: 西克西克拉藤將阿波妮波莉納衍捲上天界；她藏於太陽神伊尼伊尼特的檳榔樹間，每日以其神力把魚簽變成魚。太陽歸家見屋內如燃，原是美人容光；二人嚼檳榔定親——兩枚檳榔渣皆化無孔瑪瑙珠，證明同族，遂成婚。她堅持隨他昇空，炎熱將她熔為油；太陽把她封入瓶中，拋回卡奧達南泉邊——她終於歸家。

sensitivity.note: Tinguian epic-cycle narrative recorded 1903-1908 by Fay-Cooper Cole among the Tinguian and published 1915; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Tinguian communities. The betel-quid divination that proves kinship is a Tinguian marriage custom.

passages.text: Aponibolinayen and her sister-in-law Dinay went to gather siksiklat greens; as soon as she began to break off the siksiklat she saw, it encircled and carried her up, and when they reached the sky the vine placed her below the alosip tree by a spring whose sands were oday beads and whose betel-nut tree was gold. The owner of the little house near the well was Ini-init, the Sun — but he was not there, because he had gone up to make the sun, which was his work in the daytime. The next morning Aponibolinayen followed him into his house and quickly cooked, using her magic power: she took the stick used for roasting fish and cooked it, and the fish-stick became cut-up fish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When afternoon came Ini-init went home after fishing, and saw that his house appeared as if it was burning — but it was not burning: what looked like flame at the place of his bed was a very pretty lady. He cooked, and she awoke to see the handsome man cutting fish; the pot she had cooked in looked like a rooster's egg, and the rice she had cooked was one grain of broken rice, and because of all this Ini-init was surprised — and the woman vanished into the leaves of the betel-nut where she hid. Next morning he went up again to make the sun; when afternoon came, his food was cooked though no one was in the house, and he resolved to hide and watch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At sunset he sent the big star to follow him in the sky, and went home to spy on the woman; he slammed shut the door and reached the woman cooking, who cried, 'You cut me only once, so that I only cure one time, if you are the old enemy.' 'If I were the old enemy, I should have cut before,' said Ini-init, and he sat near her. He arranged the betel-nut covered with gold for them to chew, since it is bad to talk who do not know each other's names; when she laid down her quid it looked like an agate bead with no hole for the thread, and the quid of Ini-init looked like a square bead — and when both quids had this form they knew they were relatives. 'My name is Ini-init, who often goes to travel over the world. I always stop in the afternoon. What can I do, it is my business,' he said; 'My name is Aponibolinayen, who lives in Kaodanan, who am the sister of Awig,' she said. 'We are relatives, and it is good for us to be married. Do not be afraid even though you did not come here of your own accord.' Then they married.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When it became the middle of the night, Aponibolinayen woke and said she would go up with him in the early morning; 'Do not come, for it is very hot up above... you will repent when we are there,' said Ini-init, but she answered and answered until he agreed, and they arranged many blankets and pillows to go under. They went east, and when they arrived there the sun shone, and Aponibolinayen became oil because it was so hot; Ini-init put her in a bottle, corked it, covered it with blankets and pillows, and dropped it down. She fell by the well in Kaodanan, and Indiapan, who was dipping water, unwrapped the bundle and found a pretty lady — none equal to her — and ran to the town crying that Aponibolinayen, whom they had long sought at the cost of many cows, had fallen by the spring; and her father and mother went quickly down to the well and found the daughter they had sought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Baby from the Itching Finger and the Betel-Nuts That Grow on Knees

region.en: Kaodanan and Nagbotobotan (Tinguian mythic towns), Abra Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋阿布拉省卡奧達南與納格博托博坦（丁桂安神話城鎮，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tinguian oral epic-cycle tale; collected 1903-1908, published 1915 (Fay-Cooper Cole)

source.work: Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian: A Study in Philippine Folk-Lore (Field Museum, 1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (conclusion), pp. 38-41

summary.en: Back home, Aponibolinayen feels her little finger itch; her mother pricks it and a pretty baby pops out. At the balaua ceremony the gold-covered betel-nuts are oiled and sent to invite the whole world — any who refuse will have the nut grow on their knee — and old Alokotan guesses the father: 'You invited all the people except Ini-init, who is above. Perhaps he made Aponibolinayen pregnant, because the siksiklat took her up.' The summoned Sun first lets the betel-nut grow on his head, then on his pig, before he comes; at the gate the baby springs to him, and the round stone that carries it turns into a man — the Sun — who builds the balaua and pays the marriage price.
summary.zh: 歸家後阿波妮波莉納衍小指發癢，母親一刺，俏嬰跳出。巴勞瓦大宴上，裹金檳榔受油後奉命邀請全世界——不來者，檳榔便在其膝上生根。老嫗阿洛科坦一語道破：『你們誰都請了，就是沒請天上的伊尼伊尼特——西克西克拉藤捲她上天時，許是他使她有孕。』太陽先任檳榔長在頭上、再長在豬頭上，方才應召；嬰兒在他近門時歡喜撲去，而抱嬰的圓石滾動間化作人形——正是太陽。他建巴勞瓦、付聘禮。

sensitivity.note: Tinguian epic-cycle narrative recorded 1903-1908 by Fay-Cooper Cole; archival record. The betel-nut compulsion and quid omens are Tinguian ritual conventions; the balaua and Sayang ceremonies are named, not described operationally.

passages.text: Back in Kaodanan, Aponibolinayen commanded them to prick her little finger, which itched; and when her mother pricked it, out popped a pretty baby. Her mother asked where she got the baby, but Aponibolinayen only said, 'I do not know where I got it, and I did not feel.' 'Ala, we make balaua to-morrow,' said the father and mother. They built the balaua, and Ebang used magic so that many people went to pound rice for them; then they went to get the betel-nut which is covered with gold for chewing, and when these arrived Ebang oiled them in the dark: 'You betel-nuts go to all the people in the whole world and invite them. If any of them do not come, you grow on their knees.' And those betel-nuts went to invite all the people in the whole world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (conclusion); not verbatim.

passages.text: The betel-nut that went to Nagbotobotan, the place where the old woman Alokotan lived, told her of the invitation — 'I wait for you, for if you do not come, I shall grow on your knee' — and it took her up. At the festival no one wanted the baby to go to them, for none wished it to approach; then the old woman Alokotan summoned the spirits and said, 'You invited all the people except Ini-init, who is above. You did not send the prepared betel-nut covered with gold to summon him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (conclusion); not verbatim.

passages.text: Perhaps he made Aponibolinayen pregnant, because the siksiklat took her up when they went to gather greens.' So they oiled and sent betel-nuts, and the one that arrived above said, 'Good morning, Sun, I do not tarry. If you do not wish to come, I will grow on your head.' 'Grow on my head, I do not wish to go,' said the Sun — and the betel-nut jumped up and grew, until it became so tall the Sun could not carry it and was in pain; 'You go to my pig, that is what you grow on,' he said, and the pig began to squeal under the weight. 'Ala! get off my big pig and I come,' said Ini-init, and the betel-nut got off the pig.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (conclusion); not verbatim.

passages.text: When they came, Pagatipanan carried the baby near the gate, and as Ini-init and the betel-nut approached, the baby was happy and went to be carried by Ini-init. At the festival place the people saw that he who carried the baby rolled, because he was round, and that he was not a man but a stone; Ebang and Pagatipanan told Aponibolinayen to take off her arm beads and dress in rags, wrapping her wrists with strings, so that she could go with the stone when he took her to his home. She obeyed, and after the balaua was finished they went away to the town of the stone — and there the sun became a man, he who had been a stone before. 'When next month comes we shall build balaua, Aponibolinayen, so that we can invite our relatives, and I will pay the marriage price, because I marry you,' said Ini-init. They summoned the old woman Alokotan to start the balaua, and sang da-eng; the gold-covered betel-nuts went out again to invite the relatives, growing on the knee of anyone who refused, until all had come to the Sayang with the stone and Aponibolinayen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (conclusion); not verbatim.
